introduction: These figures come from the annual audit reports of the Commission on Audit (COA) for each city and municipal government in Cagayan. A figure appears only after it has been checked against its report.

notes.title: How to Read the Table
notes.text: Each row is one line as COA prints it, and each column is a fiscal year, from oldest to newest. An arrow compares a figure with the year before: up for an increase, down for a decrease. It does not say whether the change is good or bad. A loss is shown in parentheses. Shortened amounts such as ₱1.2B show the exact amount when you hover over, focus on or tap them. Select a year to open its Yearly Summary.

notes.title: Where the Figures Come From
notes.text: Totals come from the Executive Summary of each COA Annual Audit Report. A team member checks each figure against the report before it is shown, or it is shown when two COA reports print the same amount or amounts no more than ₱1.00 apart. The newest year is shown from its own report until the next year's report confirms or restates it. The COA Sources list under the table opens each report at the cited page.

notes.title: Sum of Reporting Towns
notes.text: The total of the city and municipal governments that reported for a year. It is not the accounts of the Provincial Government. The coverage note says how many of the 29 governments reported, and the change compares only governments that reported in both years.

notes.title: What These Figures Are Not
notes.text: These are the accounts of local governments. They are not the sales of private businesses, the size of the local economy or a rating of a government. Part of every town's income is its share of national taxes, which can rise or fall without any change in local business activity.

budgetSteps.text: The council approves how much may be spent and for what, in the annual appropriation ordinance. This is permission to spend, not spending.
Part of the approved amount is released to offices so they can start committing it.
An office commits the money through a contract, a salary or a purchase order. The government is now bound to pay.
The government pays the cash. The Executive Summary does not print this step.

topics.title: Financial Condition
topics.summary: What the government owned and owed on December 31.

metrics.label: Assets
metrics.meaning: Everything the government owns, such as cash, amounts owed to it, land, buildings and roads.
metrics.why: It shows the resources the government holds to deliver services and build infrastructure.

metrics.label: Liabilities
metrics.meaning: Everything the government owes, such as unpaid bills, loans and money it holds for others.
metrics.why: Compared with Assets, it shows how much of what the government holds is owed to others.

metrics.label: Government Equity
metrics.meaning: Assets minus Liabilities. No one owns shares in a government; this is what remains after its debts.
metrics.why: A steady or rising amount shows a government that is not living on borrowed resources.

topics.title: Results of Operation
topics.summary: The income the government earned in the year and the expenses it recorded, including costs that involve no cash, such as depreciation.

metrics.label: Income
metrics.meaning: All income of the government for the year, including its share of national taxes. It is not the income of businesses.
metrics.why: It is the size of the resources the government had to work with.

metrics.label: Expenses
metrics.meaning: The costs the government recorded for the year, including salaries, operations, depreciation and transfers. It is not the same as cash paid.
metrics.why: It shows the cost of running the government and its services.

metrics.label: Net Income
metrics.meaning: Income minus Expenses. A loss is shown in parentheses.
metrics.why: A surplus means the year's income covered its expenses; a loss means it did not.

topics.title: Budget Execution
topics.summary: How the approved budget moved from approval to commitment. See How a Budget Is Spent.

metrics.label: Current Appropriations
metrics.meaning: The most the government may spend this year, approved by the Sangguniang Bayan or Sangguniang Panlungsod in the annual appropriation ordinance.
metrics.why: It shows what the government planned to spend for the year.

metrics.label: Current Allotments
metrics.meaning: The part of this year's appropriations released to offices for use.
metrics.why: It shows how much of the approved budget offices were allowed to commit.

metrics.label: Continuing Allotments
metrics.meaning: Budget approved in an earlier year that remains available, usually for projects not yet finished.
metrics.why: It shows past commitments still being carried out.

metrics.label: Current Obligations
metrics.meaning: Amounts the government legally committed to pay this year, through contracts, salaries and purchase orders.
metrics.why: Compared with appropriations, it shows how much of the approved budget was actually put to work.

metrics.label: Continuing Obligations
metrics.meaning: Commitments made this year against budget carried over from earlier years.
metrics.why: It shows progress on projects funded in earlier years.

topics.title: Business Activity Over Time
topics.summary: Annual registered business activity for one industry or Business Category. Shown only with simulated records.

metrics.label: Active Businesses
metrics.meaning: Businesses recorded as new or renewed for the year.
metrics.why: It shows how many businesses were operating.
metrics.formula: Count of new and renewed business-year records.

metrics.label: New Registrations
metrics.meaning: Businesses newly registered in the year.
metrics.why: It shows how many businesses started.

metrics.label: Closed Businesses
metrics.meaning: Businesses formally closed in the year.
metrics.why: It shows how many businesses stopped operating.
